content: Diabetes mellitus is associated with a range of cardiovascular complications, which can be categorized into microvascular and macrovascular diseases. Microvascular complications involve damage to small blood vessels, while macrovascular complications affect larger arteries. Chronic hyperglycemia, or elevated blood glucose levels, leads to vascular damage, known as angiopathy. Endothelial cells in blood vessels absorb excess glucose, as they do not rely on insulin for glucose uptake. This results in the overproduction of surface glycoproteins and thickening of the basement membrane, which weakens the blood vessels. These changes underlie the development of both microvascular and macrovascular complications. Microvascular Disease Damage to small blood vessels, or microangiopathy, can result in several specific complications: 1. Diabetic Retinopathy: This condition involves the growth of fragile, low-quality new blood vessels in the retina, as well as macular edema (swelling of the macula). These changes can lead to significant vision loss or blindness. Retinal damage caused by microangiopathy is the leading cause of blindness among non-elderly adults in the United States. 2. Diabetic Neuropathy: This refers to abnormal or reduced sensation, often presenting in a glove and stocking distribution, starting with the feet and potentially affecting other nerves, including those in the hands and fingers. Neuropathy, when combined with vascular damage, can lead to complications such as diabetic foot. Other forms of diabetic neuropathy include mononeuritis, autonomic neuropathy, and diabetic amyotrophy, which causes muscle weakness due to nerve damage. 3. Diabetic Nephropathy: This involves kidney damage that can progress to chronic renal failure, ultimately requiring dialysis. Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of kidney failure in adults worldwide, particularly in developed countries. Macrovascular Disease Macrovascular complications involve damage to larger arteries and contribute to cardiovascular diseases, often accelerated by atherosclerosis. These include: 1. Coronary Artery Disease (CAD): This can manifest as angina or myocardial infarction (heart attack). 2. Stroke: Diabetes increases the risk of ischemic stroke. 3. Peripheral Vascular Disease (PVD): This condition can cause intermittent claudication, characterized by pain in the legs and feet during exertion. It also contributes to diabetic foot complications. 4. Diabetic Myonecrosis: This refers to muscle wasting associated with diabetes. Diabetic Foot: A combination of neuropathy and arterial disease can lead to skin ulcers, infections, and, in severe cases, necrosis and gangrene. Diabetic foot is a major cause of leg and foot infections and delayed wound healing in individuals with diabetes. It is the leading cause of non-traumatic amputations, particularly of toes and feet, in the developed world. Interestingly, carotid artery stenosis does not appear to occur more frequently in individuals with diabetes, and there is a lower prevalence of abdominal aortic aneurysm. However, diabetes is associated with higher morbidity, mortality, and operative risks in these conditions. Cardiovascular Disease and Gender While men with diabetes have a higher overall risk of cardiovascular disorders, women with diabetes face an even greater relative risk of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular complications compared to men with diabetes. This increased risk in women is independent of menopausal status and may be partially explained by higher levels of adipose tissue and a more active immune system in women with diabetes.
